name: Dhampus
tagline: Gurung hill village facing Machhapuchhre, 1.5 hours above Phedi
meta_description: Dhampus village guide: Gurung homestays, sunrise over Annapurna South and Machhapuchhre, the walk from Phedi, the link to Australian Camp, permits and lodges.
summary: Dhampus is a Gurung and Brahmin farming village at about 1,650 m on a ridge north-west of Pokhara. A 1.5–2 hour walk up from Phedi, or an hour by jeep road, it looks straight at Annapurna South, Hiunchuli and Machhapuchhre. It is the second night on the easy Australian Camp loop.
intro: Dhampus spreads for a couple of kilometres along a south-facing ridge, its stone houses with slate and tin roofs set among millet, maize and rice terraces. The upper village is mainly Gurung, a community known for its Gurkha soldiers, communal labour and lively songs and dances, while the lower parts are home to Brahmin and Chhetri families. Lodges and homestays sit along the main trail, many with flower gardens and terraces that face the mountains.

The panorama from the village is wide: Dhaulagiri on clear days in the far west, then Annapurna South, Hiunchuli, Annapurna I behind, Machhapuchhre and Annapurna II, with Lamjung Himal to the east. Mornings from October to March are usually clear, and sunrise from the upper village or the viewpoint above it is a highlight of any short trek near Pokhara. In the evening the same peaks turn orange, and lodge terraces fill with trekkers watching the light fade.

Dhampus has long been a stop on routes into the Annapurna region: the old trail from Phedi to Landruk and Ghandruk passed through, and it remains the start of the Mardi Himal trek's eastern approach. Today a jeep road reaches the village, but the stone trail from Phedi through forest and fields is still the better way to arrive. With Australian Camp an hour or two to the west, the two make a classic two- or three-day loop from Pokhara.
facts: ≈ 16 km to Phedi (30–40 min) + 1.5–2 h walk, or ≈ 1 h by jeep
Gurung homestays, sunrise over the Annapurnas, start of Mardi Himal trek

highlights.title: Sunrise over the Annapurnas
highlights.text: From the upper village or the small viewpoint above it, dawn lights Annapurna South, Hiunchuli and Machhapuchhre one after another. On very clear mornings Dhaulagiri glows far to the west. The view is broad and unobstructed, and you share it with village life rather than crowds.

highlights.title: Gurung village life
highlights.text: Walk the lanes between stone houses where women weave baskets and tend buffalo, children walk to school and elders sit on stone resting platforms called chautara. In harvest season the courtyards fill with drying millet and corn.

highlights.title: Homestay with a family
highlights.text: Several Dhampus families host guests in simple rooms, cook dal bhat and seasonal vegetables from their fields and invite you into the kitchen. It is a gentle introduction to rural Nepal, an hour from Pokhara's cafes.

highlights.title: The stone trail from Phedi
highlights.text: The traditional path climbs about 500 m from Phedi through forest and terraced fields in 1.5–2 hours. It is steep in places but well made, with tea shops and views opening over the Seti valley as you climb.

highlights.title: Gateway to Mardi Himal
highlights.text: Dhampus is a common starting point for the Mardi Himal trek, which climbs through Pothana and Deurali to Forest Camp, High Camp and a viewpoint above 4,000 m. Even if you are not doing the trek, walking an hour up towards Pothana gives fine forest and views.

how_to_reach.text: Phedi is about 16 km from Pokhara on the Pokhara–Baglung highway, 30–40 minutes by car. A jeep road also climbs from the highway to Dhampus, about 1 hour from Pokhara by four-wheel drive, useful for those who cannot walk far. Taxis go to Phedi; jeeps to the village are arranged in advance.

From Phedi, a stone trail climbs about 500 m to Dhampus in 1.5–2 hours. From Australian Camp, walk east via Pothana (about 1 hour) and down to Dhampus (1–1.5 hours more). Foreign trekkers need ACAP and TIMS permits and a licensed guide under current rules.

where_to_stay: Dhampus has a good choice of simple trekking lodges and homestays strung along the main trail through the village, many with garden terraces facing the mountains. Rooms are basic but clean, with twin beds and either shared or simple attached bathrooms; hot showers are usually solar or gas-heated, and meals are dal bhat, noodles, momo and Tibetan bread. A few lodges have upgraded rooms with larger windows and better bathrooms. There are no 3-star hotels. We book a view lodge or a family homestay according to your preference, and travellers wanting more comfort can visit on a day trip and return to Pokhara.
tips: Ask for a mountain-facing room on the upper floor; the view from the bed at dawn is worth it.
Walk up from Phedi in the cooler afternoon or early morning; the lower trail is sunny and warm.
Carry Nepali rupees for lodge bills, hot showers and charging, as cards are rarely accepted.
Respect village customs: ask before photographing people and remove shoes before entering homes.
Avoid the trail in the monsoon, when leeches appear in the forest and steps get slippery.

experiences.title: Gurung homestay night in Dhampus
experiences.summary: Stay with a Gurung family in Dhampus, share a home-cooked dinner of dal bhat and seasonal vegetables, learn a few words of Gurung and Nepali, and wake to the Annapurnas from the courtyard. A gentle, honest look at hill life an hour from Pokhara.
body: Homestays in Dhampus are simple family homes with one or two guest rooms, coordinated through a community group so that income is shared around the village. You arrive in the afternoon after the walk from Phedi or Australian Camp, are welcomed with tea and sometimes a marigold garland, and settle into a clean room with twin beds and warm blankets. Bathrooms are usually shared and may be outside the main house.

In the evening, join the family in the kitchen while dinner cooks over a wood fire or gas stove. Expect dal bhat with lentil soup, rice, a vegetable curry of whatever is in season, saag greens, homemade pickle and perhaps fresh buffalo-milk yoghurt. Your hosts may show you how to grind millet, weave a doko basket or make millet rotis. In some homes, children or neighbours sing Gurung songs or show a dance.

Wake at dawn to see the mountains from the courtyard, help with morning chores if you like, and eat breakfast of chapati, eggs and tea before walking on. Bring a small gift such as fruit or stationery for children rather than sweets, dress modestly and ask before taking photos. The experience suits curious travellers who are happy with simple facilities. Our guide stays nearby and can help with translation and any requests during your stay.

faqs.q: Is a homestay in Dhampus comfortable?
faqs.a: It is simple but clean. You get a private room with twin beds and blankets, home-cooked meals and a warm welcome. Bathrooms are often shared and may be squat toilets, and hot water depends on solar or gas heaters. If you need attached western bathrooms, choose one of the trekking lodges in the village instead.

faqs.q: Is a Dhampus homestay safe for solo women?
faqs.a: Yes, generally. Homestays are family homes coordinated by the community, Dhampus is a quiet village on a well-used trail, and our licensed guide stays nearby. As anywhere, use common sense, dress modestly and keep valuables with you. Many solo women travellers stay in Dhampus homestays each season.

faqs.q: What do I eat at a Gurung homestay?
faqs.a: Mainly dal bhat: rice, lentil soup, seasonal vegetable curry, greens and pickle, often with yoghurt or buttermilk. Breakfast is usually chapati or Tibetan bread with eggs and tea. Meat is occasionally offered. Vegetarian meals are easy; tell your guide about Jain or other dietary needs in advance.

experiences.title: Sunrise over Annapurna South from Dhampus
experiences.summary: A short walk from your lodge to the upper village or viewpoint at dawn, where the sun lights Annapurna South, Hiunchuli, Machhapuchhre and on clear days Dhaulagiri. Wider than the view from Australian Camp and with village roofs in the foreground.
body: Dhampus faces the mountains across the deep valley of the Modi and Mardi rivers, so it looks at the Annapurna range almost side-on, from Dhaulagiri in the west to Lamjung Himal in the east. Ask your lodge the evening before which spot is best; usually it is the upper village or a small rise above it, 5–15 minutes' walk from most lodges. Lodges in the upper part of the village often have the view straight from their terraces.

Be in place 20 minutes before sunrise. The first light touches the tallest summits, Dhaulagiri and Annapurna I, then slides down to Annapurna South, Hiunchuli and Machhapuchhre's twin peak. Below, mist often lies in the valleys while smoke rises from village kitchens. Roosters, prayer bells and the clink of milk cans are the soundtrack. In October and November, terraces of ripening millet and rice glow gold in the first light, adding colour to the foreground of your photographs.

October to December gives the most reliable clear mornings; January and February are clear but cold. From March the views soften in haze, though rhododendrons bloom in the forest above the village. After sunrise, breakfast at your lodge before walking down to Phedi, or continue to Australian Camp or towards Pothana. Pack your camera, a warm jacket and a torch the night before so you can leave quickly. On cloudy mornings, wait 20–30 minutes before giving up, as gaps in the cloud are common.

faqs.q: Which mountains can you see from Dhampus?
faqs.a: On clear mornings: Dhaulagiri far to the west, Annapurna South, Hiunchuli, Annapurna I, Machhapuchhre, Annapurna II and Lamjung Himal. Mardi Himal is visible on Machhapuchhre's flank. The panorama is widest from the upper village. Views are clearest from October to December.

faqs.q: Dhampus or Australian Camp: which has the better view?
faqs.a: Australian Camp is higher at about 2,060 m and closer to Machhapuchhre, with an open meadow foreground. Dhampus, at about 1,650 m, has a wider panorama including Dhaulagiri on clear days and village houses in the foreground. Doing both on one trek gives you two different sunrises.

faqs.q: Do I need to walk far for sunrise in Dhampus?
faqs.a: No. Most lodges have a mountain view from their terrace, and the best viewpoints in the upper village are 5–15 minutes' walk. Bring a torch for the walk in the dark and a warm jacket, as mornings from December to February are close to freezing.

experiences.title: Phedi to Dhampus stone trail walk
experiences.price_hint: Included in our Australian Camp and Dhampus trek
experiences.summary: The classic approach to Dhampus: a stone staircase from Phedi on the Baglung highway, climbing about 500 m through forest, terraces and hamlets with widening views over the Seti valley. Short, steep in places and full of village life.
body: Phedi, whose name simply means the foot of the hill, is a cluster of shops at about 1,130 m on the Pokhara–Baglung highway, 30–40 minutes from Lakeside. The trail starts behind the shops and climbs straight up the hillside on stone steps, crossing the jeep road a few times. The first 30 minutes are the steepest, through scrub forest with a few tea shops for breathers. Fill water bottles at Phedi before you start.

Higher up, the path eases through terraced fields of millet and rice, past farmhouses and resting platforms shaded by large pipal and banyan trees. Look back over the Seti valley towards Pokhara and Sarangkot, and ahead for the first glimpses of Machhapuchhre. The full climb gains about 500 m and takes 1.5–2 hours at a steady pace. Village children walk the trail to school, and families carry fodder and firewood in doko baskets, which gives the walk a lived-in feel.

On our trek you walk this trail downhill on the last morning, which takes 1–1.5 hours and is harder on the knees than the legs; walking poles help. It is a good trail for children and seniors who walk at their own pace. Start early from March to May to avoid the heat on the open lower section, and avoid it during heavy monsoon rain. A porter can carry overnight bags if you prefer to walk light.

faqs.q: How long is the walk from Phedi to Dhampus?
faqs.a: About 1.5–2 hours uphill, gaining roughly 500 m from about 1,130 m to 1,650 m on stone steps and paths. The descent takes 1–1.5 hours. Fit walkers do it faster. The trail crosses the jeep road a few times, so a vehicle can meet anyone who tires.

faqs.q: Can I drive to Dhampus instead of walking?
faqs.a: Yes. A jeep road reaches the village from the Baglung highway, about 1 hour from Pokhara by four-wheel drive. It is rough in places and can be closed after heavy rain. This is useful for seniors or anyone who wants the village and view without the climb.

faqs.q: Is the Phedi to Dhampus trail suitable for kids?
faqs.a: Yes, for children of about six and older who are used to walking. The steps are steep in the first section, so take breaks at the tea shops. Make sure children wear proper shoes and carry water. A porter can carry the family's overnight bags.

faqs.q: What is the altitude of Dhampus?
faqs.a: About 1,650 m, roughly 830 m above Pokhara Lakeside and 500 m above Phedi on the Baglung highway. At this height altitude sickness is not a concern for healthy travellers. Nights in winter are cool, around 2–6 °C, so bring a warm layer.

faqs.q: How far is Dhampus from Pokhara?
faqs.a: Phedi, the trailhead, is about 16 km from Pokhara, 30–40 minutes by car; from there it is 1.5–2 hours on foot. By jeep road, Dhampus is about 1 hour from Pokhara. From Australian Camp, the walk via Pothana takes 2–2.5 hours.

faqs.q: Is Dhampus worth an overnight stay?
faqs.a: Yes. Sunset and sunrise over the Annapurnas, a quiet Gurung village and simple lodges or homestays make it one of the best easy overnights near Pokhara. Combined with Australian Camp it forms a two- or three-day trek that suits families, seniors and first-time trekkers.

faqs.q: Do I need a permit for Dhampus?
faqs.a: Yes. Dhampus is within the Annapurna Conservation Area, so trekkers need an ACAP entry permit. Foreign trekkers also need a TIMS card and, under rules introduced in 2023, a licensed guide. SAARC nationals pay a reduced ACAP fee. Check current status before you travel.

faqs.q: Is Dhampus on the Mardi Himal trek?
faqs.a: Yes. Dhampus is a common starting point for the Mardi Himal trek, which climbs north via Pothana and Deurali to Forest Camp, Low Camp, High Camp and a viewpoint at about 4,500 m. Many Mardi Himal treks spend their first night in or near Dhampus.

faqs.q: Are there good lodges in Dhampus?
faqs.a: Dhampus has a good range of simple trekking lodges and homestays with twin rooms, garden terraces and mountain views, plus a few lodges with upgraded rooms and attached bathrooms. There are no star-rated hotels. Book ahead in October and November, the busiest months.

Yes. Seniors who cannot manage the 1.5–2 hour climb from Phedi can reach the village by jeep in about an hour from Pokhara, stay overnight in a lodge with a view and enjoy sunrise without a long walk. Bring medicines and warm clothing for cold nights.

faqs.q: What is the best season to visit Dhampus?
faqs.a: October to December gives the clearest mountain views and dry trails. February to April is mild with rhododendrons flowering above the village. June to September is the monsoon, with clouds hiding the peaks and leeches on the trails, so we do not recommend it.

faqs.q: Can I do Dhampus as a day trip from Pokhara?
faqs.a: Yes. Drive to Phedi early, walk up to Dhampus in 1.5–2 hours, have lunch with a view and walk down in the afternoon, back in Pokhara by evening. Morning views are usually clearer, so a day trip risks clouds by midday. An overnight is better for photography.
